questions.questionText: What does a LangGraph checkpointer actually do?
options: It persists graph state after every step, keyed by a thread_id, so a conversation can be resumed later even across restarts
It validates the graph's structure at compile time
It automatically retries failed tool calls
questions.correctAnswer: It persists graph state after every step, keyed by a thread_id, so a conversation can be resumed later even across restarts
questions.explanation: Without a checkpointer, state exists only for one invoke() call; a checkpointer saves it externally (e.g. to Postgres) so the same thread_id can pick up where it left off.

questions.questionText: What's the difference between streamMode "updates" and streamMode "messages"?
options: "updates" emits one event per completed node; "messages" streams individual LLM tokens as they're generated
"messages" is only for text input, "updates" is only for tool calls
questions.correctAnswer: "updates" emits one event per completed node; "messages" streams individual LLM tokens as they're generated
questions.explanation: "updates" is useful for showing which node is currently running (e.g. highlighting an agent graph UI); "messages" is what powers token-by-token chat UI streaming.

questions.questionText: Why might a production chat agent want both persistence and streaming at the same time?
options: They solve the same problem so only one is ever needed
Persistence makes conversations resumable across sessions, while streaming shows progress within a single run — most real products need both
Streaming replaces the need for a checkpointer entirely
They cannot be used together in LangGraph
questions.correctAnswer: Persistence makes conversations resumable across sessions, while streaming shows progress within a single run — most real products need both
questions.explanation: The two features address different UX problems (resuming later vs. feeling responsive now) and compose naturally — a checkpointed graph can still stream its current run's progress.
